body:
What is biotechnology?

Biotechnology is the use of living organisms, cells, enzymes or other biological components to produce useful goods and services. Humans have used microorganisms to prepare curd, bread and fermented foods for centuries. Modern biotechnology extends these principles to the production of medicines, industrial enzymes, fuels, improved crops and environmental treatment systems.

Biotechnology does not always involve genetic modification. A naturally occurring bacterium that converts milk into curd is being used in biotechnology, even though its DNA has not been deliberately changed. Similarly, microorganisms can help clean wastewater or improve soil fertility without being genetically engineered.

Industrial biotechnology uses biological systems to manufacture chemicals, fuels, materials and other products. Environmental biotechnology uses biological systems to prevent, reduce or treat pollution. Agricultural biotechnology applies biological methods to improve crops, manage pests and support agricultural production.

How a biological production system works

Most biotechnology applications involve 3 basic elements: a biological agent, a suitable raw material and a useful outcome. The biological agent may be an entire microorganism or an enzyme isolated from it. The raw material may be sugar, plant biomass, organic waste or another substance that the biological agent can transform.

For example, yeast converts sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide under suitable conditions. In a different application, selected bacteria and fungi consume organic matter during wastewater treatment. The underlying principle is similar: a biological process changes the original material into a different substance or a less harmful form.

Traditional and modern biotechnology

ApproachMain principleExample
Traditional biotechnologyUses naturally occurring biological activitiesCurd and bread preparation
Industrial biotechnologyUses organisms or enzymes for controlled productionEnzyme and bioethanol production
Genetic engineeringDeliberately alters genetic materialBt cotton
Synthetic biologyDesigns or redesigns biological functionsEngineered microbial sensing systems

These categories overlap. Genetic engineering may be used within industrial biotechnology, while synthetic biology may be used to develop new biological production systems. However, neither genetic engineering nor synthetic biology is necessary for every biotechnology application.

Biotechnology and sustainability

Many biological processes can use renewable raw materials such as crop residues, food-processing waste and other forms of biomass. This creates opportunities to reduce waste and replace some products derived from fossil resources. Nevertheless, a product is not automatically environmentally beneficial merely because microorganisms or plants are involved. Its environmental performance also depends on land use, energy consumption, water requirements, transport and waste disposal.

Prelims focus

  • Biotechnology can use organisms, cells or enzymes.
  • Traditional fermentation is biotechnology even without genetic modification.
  • Industrial biotechnology produces useful substances; environmental biotechnology addresses pollution.
  • Genetic engineering changes genetic material, while synthetic biology can redesign broader biological functions.
  • Trap: Not every biotechnology product is genetically modified or environmentally sustainable.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 11, 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', §11.1; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 10, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', §§10.1–10.4; National Human Genome Research Institute, 'Synthetic Biology', introductory definition and applications, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Biotechnology: Using Living Systems to Produce Useful Products

body:
Enzymes are biological catalysts

An enzyme is a biological catalyst that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being permanently consumed by that reaction. Most enzymes are proteins, although some RNA molecules, called ribozymes, can also act as catalysts. Enzymes help biological reactions proceed rapidly under comparatively mild conditions.

An enzyme acts on a substance called its substrate. The substrate interacts with a particular region of the enzyme known as its active site. Because the active site has specific chemical and structural properties, an enzyme generally acts on a particular substrate or a limited group of related substrates.

Enzyme activity depends on conditions such as temperature and pH. Each enzyme has a range within which it functions effectively. Excessive heat can alter the structure of many protein enzymes, reducing or destroying their activity. Some enzymes also require non-protein components called cofactors.

Enzyme specificity explains why a starch-digesting enzyme cannot automatically replace a fat-digesting enzyme. The substrate and the reaction determine which enzyme is useful.

Important industrial enzymes

EnzymeSubstance acted uponImportant application
AmylaseStarchProduction of sugars from starch
ProteaseProteinsDetergents and protein processing
LipaseFats and oilsRemoval of oily stains in detergents
CellulaseCelluloseProcessing plant-based materials
PectinasePectinClarification of fruit juices

Many industrial enzymes are obtained from microorganisms because microorganisms can be cultivated for production. Enzymes may be used after extraction, or microorganisms may carry out the desired reactions directly.

Fermentation: microorganisms transform raw materials

Fermentation commonly refers to the metabolic conversion of sugars into substances such as ethanol or organic acids. In classical alcoholic fermentation, yeast obtains energy from sugars and produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, usually under oxygen-limited conditions.

The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is associated with bread-making and ethanol production. In bread dough, the released carbon dioxide contributes to rising. In bioethanol production, ethanol is the desired fuel product.

Lactic acid bacteria, including species of Lactobacillus, convert suitable sugars into lactic acid. Their activity helps transform milk into curd. The acid changes the properties of milk proteins, causing the characteristic texture of curd.

The term industrial fermentation is also used more broadly for controlled cultivation of microorganisms to manufacture useful products. Such industrial processes are not necessarily oxygen-free. For example, production of certain microbial chemicals and enzymes may require oxygen.

Named microorganisms and useful products

  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae: ethanol production and bread-making.
  • Aspergillus niger: industrial production of citric acid.
  • Acetobacter aceti: conversion of ethanol into acetic acid under aerobic conditions.
  • Lactic acid bacteria: preparation of curd and other fermented foods.

From a biological reaction to a marketable product

Industrial production requires an appropriate environment for the selected organism or enzyme. A bioreactor is a vessel in which biological conversion occurs under controlled conditions. The production stage is followed by separation, purification and other necessary operations collectively called downstream processing.

A bioreactor is therefore a production vessel, not a particular microorganism. Downstream processing is the subsequent recovery and preparation of the desired product, not the biological conversion itself.

Prelims focus

  • Most enzymes are proteins; catalytic RNA molecules are called ribozymes.
  • Amylase acts on starch, protease on proteins and lipase on fats.
  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae is used in alcoholic fermentation.
  • Aspergillus niger is associated with citric acid production.
  • Bioreactors support production; downstream processing recovers and prepares the product.
  • Trap: Industrial fermentation is not always an anaerobic process.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 11, ch. 9, 'Biomolecules', section on enzymes; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 10, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', §§10.1–10.2; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 11, 'Biotechnology: Principles and Processes', §11.3; NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 2, 'Microorganisms: Friend and Foe'.]

title: Enzymes and Fermentation in Industrial Biotechnology

body:
What makes a fuel a biofuel?

A biofuel is a fuel derived from biomass or recently living biological material. Biomass may include sugar-rich crops, plant oils, agricultural residues, cattle dung and other organic wastes. Biofuels can be gaseous, liquid or solid, depending on their composition and method of production.

The source of the raw material and the biological or chemical transformation must be distinguished. Not all biofuels are produced by fermentation. Some use microbial processes, while others require chemical processing of plant- or animal-derived materials.

Bioethanol

Bioethanol is ethanol produced from biological feedstocks. Yeast can ferment sugars to obtain ethanol. Sugarcane molasses is a familiar example of a sugar-rich industrial feedstock. Starch-containing materials can also be used after their starch is converted into fermentable sugars.

Feedstocks are often grouped by their origin:

  • First-generation bioethanol: uses sugar- or starch-rich agricultural crops and their products.
  • Second-generation bioethanol: uses lignocellulosic biomass such as agricultural residues and other non-food plant material. Cellulose and related components must first become accessible for conversion into useful sugars.

Second-generation fuels can use material that might otherwise be discarded, but their environmental advantage still depends on collection, processing and energy requirements.

Biogas

Biogas is a combustible gas mixture formed when microorganisms break down suitable organic material in the absence of oxygen. The process is called anaerobic digestion. It involves several groups of microorganisms, including methane-producing microorganisms known as methanogens.

Methanobacterium is a textbook example of a methanogen. Methanogens are also found in the rumen of cattle and in anaerobic sludge digesters.

Biogas contains mainly methane and carbon dioxide, with smaller amounts of other gases. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy describes typical raw biogas as containing approximately 55–65% methane and 35–44% carbon dioxide, with traces of other gases. Actual composition varies with feedstock and operating conditions.

Methane is the principal combustible component. The remaining digested material, called digestate or spent slurry, can be used as a source of plant nutrients when suitable for agricultural application. Thus, a biogas system can produce both fuel and a potentially useful agricultural residue.

Biogas and compressed biogas

Raw biogas is not the same as compressed biogas (CBG). CBG is produced after biogas has been upgraded to a methane-rich gas and compressed for suitable uses. Removing much of the carbon dioxide and undesirable impurities improves its fuel characteristics.

Biodiesel

Biodiesel is a liquid fuel generally produced by chemically converting suitable plant oils or animal fats into fatty-acid esters. It is therefore incorrect to assume that biodiesel is always obtained by yeast fermentation. Biodiesel and bioethanol are different fuels with different feedstocks and production routes.

FuelTypical feedstockPrincipal conversion
BioethanolSugars or starch-derived sugarsMicrobial fermentation
BiogasCattle dung and organic wasteAnaerobic microbial digestion
BiodieselPlant oils or animal fatsConversion into fatty-acid esters

India's National Bioenergy Programme

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy notified the National Bioenergy Programme on 2 November 2022. Its published Phase I covered FY 2021–22 to FY 2025–26, a period ending on 31 March 2026. The programme included components dealing with biogas, biomass and waste-to-energy. This stated Phase I period should not be interpreted as evidence of a further extension.

Prelims focus

  • Bioethanol can be produced by yeast fermentation of suitable sugars.
  • Second-generation bioethanol can use agricultural residues and other lignocellulosic biomass.
  • Biogas is produced through anaerobic digestion; methane is its main combustible component.
  • Methanogens include Methanobacterium.
  • MNRE notified the National Bioenergy Programme on 2 November 2022.
  • Trap: Biodiesel is not simply another name for fermented ethanol.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, ch. 10, 'Microbes in Human Welfare', §§10.2 and 10.4; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, 'Biogas Programme', sections on gas composition and Phase I period, consulted 13 November 2026; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, 'National Bioenergy Programme', notification dated 2 November 2022.]

title: Biofuels: Energy from Biomass and Microbial Activity

body:
Biobased materials and biodegradable materials

Biotechnology can help produce polymers and other materials from renewable biological raw materials. A polymer is a substance made of many repeating molecular units. Conventional plastics such as polyethylene are polymers, and some polymers can be produced partly or wholly from biomass-derived substances.

The word bioplastic is used in different ways. It may describe a plastic made from biological resources, a plastic capable of biodegradation under specified conditions, or a material with both properties. These meanings must not be treated as identical.

Biobased describes where a material comes from. Biodegradable describes its capacity to undergo biological degradation under particular conditions. A biobased material is not necessarily biodegradable, and a biodegradable material is not necessarily biobased.

Examples of commonly discussed polymers

MaterialBiological originDegradation characteristic
Bio-PECan be made from biomass-derived feedstocksNot inherently biodegradable
PLACan be made from biomass-derived lactic acidDegradation generally requires suitable conditions, often industrial composting
PHACan be produced by microorganismsCan biodegrade under suitable conditions, depending on the material and environment
PBATConventionally derived from fossil-based feedstocksDesigned to biodegrade under specified conditions

Polylactic acid (PLA) is a useful example of how biological and industrial processes can be combined. Lactic acid may be obtained from fermentation of suitable biological feedstocks and then used to make a polymer. Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) are another group of polymers associated with microbial production.

Neither PLA nor PHA should be assumed to disappear rapidly in every natural environment. The rate and extent of degradation depend on the particular polymer, temperature, moisture, microbial activity and disposal conditions.

Biodegradation, composting and recycling

Biodegradation involves biological activity that breaks down a material. Composting is a managed biological process that converts suitable organic materials into a compost-like product under appropriate conditions. A material advertised as compostable may require an industrial composting facility and may not degrade effectively in ordinary soil, rivers or the sea.

Recycling is different from biodegradation. Recycling generally recovers a material for further use or processing, while biodegradation changes the material through biological activity. Different plastics may require separate collection and treatment routes.

What is a circular bioeconomy?

A bioeconomy uses biological resources, biological knowledge and biological processes to produce goods and services. A circular bioeconomy additionally seeks to keep resources useful for longer, reduce waste and recover value from biological residues.

For example, agricultural residues may be used to produce a valuable chemical or fuel. Suitable remaining organic material may then enter another recovery process, such as anaerobic digestion or composting. Nutrients may eventually be returned to agricultural systems where safe and appropriate.

This approach differs from a purely linear system in which raw materials are extracted, used once and discarded. However, using renewable feedstocks does not by itself guarantee low pollution or low greenhouse-gas emissions. A sound comparison considers the product's full life cycle, including cultivation, manufacture, use and final disposal.

The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry cautions that the term bioplastic can misleadingly suggest environmental superiority. A more precise term such as biobased polymer is preferable when the origin of the material is the fact being described.

Prelims focus

  • Biobased refers to raw-material origin; biodegradable refers to degradation behaviour.
  • Bio-PE is an example of a biobased plastic that is not inherently biodegradable.
  • PLA and PHA are examples of polymers that can be made from biological resources.
  • Some biodegradable plastics, including conventional PBAT, can be fossil-based.
  • A circular bioeconomy emphasises resource recovery and repeated productive use.
  • Trap: Compostable does not necessarily mean biodegradable in every natural environment.

[Sources: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, Gold Book, entries 'bioplastic', 'biobased' and 'biodegradable polymer', consulted 13 November 2026; European Environment Agency, 'Pathways towards Circular Plastics in Europe', section 'Biobased plastic is not always biodegradable', consulted 13 November 2026; European Environment Agency, 'Global bio-based plastics production capacity', definitions and material categories, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Bioplastics and the Circular Bioeconomy
